claims.evidence: Inferred from enhanced NF-κB signaling and target gene expression in YOD1 knock-down iBMDM (Figure 4G, 4H).

claims.claim: Two independent YOD1 KO HeLa cell clones (#6 and #33) were generated using CRISPR/Cas9 technology.
claims.source: The approach yielded two independent HeLa cell clones (#6 and #33) that carry the expected genomic deletion as verified by sequencing.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by PCR, Western blot, and sequencing analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Reconstituted YOD1 binds to TRAF6 in unstimulated YOD1 KO cells.
claims.source: Co-IP revealed binding of reconstituted YOD1 to TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and the interaction was reduced after IL-1β stimulation (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: YOD1/TRAF6 interaction is reduced after IL-1β stimulation in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells.
claims.source: Co-IP revealed binding of reconstituted YOD1 to TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and the interaction was reduced after IL-1β stimulation (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation at different time points after IL-1β stimulation shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: YOD1 reconstitution in YOD1 KO cells reduces NF-κB target gene expression after IL-1β stimulation.
claims.source: On the level of NF-κB target gene expression we could verify the negative regulatory influence of YOD1 on gene induction as previously seen upon YOD1 overexpression or knock-down in HeLa cells (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: Activation of NF-κB DNA binding in response to IL-1β stimulation is reduced in YOD1 expressing cells compared to YOD1 KO cells.
claims.source: As expected for a putative negative regulator that controls TRAF6-dependent upstream signaling, activation of NF-κB DNA binding in response to IL-1β stimulation was reduced in YOD1 expressing HeLa cells.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Phosphorylation and degradation of IκBα is reduced in YOD1 expressing cells compared to YOD1 KO cells after IL-1β stimulation.
claims.source: In line, phosphorylation and degradation of the NF-κB inhibitor IκBα was reduced in YOD1 expressing cells (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: Reconstitution of two independent YOD1 KO cell clones provides evidence that YOD1 counteracts NF-κB signaling upon IL-1β stimulation.
claims.source: Thus, reconstitution of two independent KO cell clones provided clear evidence that YOD1 counteracts NF-κB signaling upon IL-1β stimulation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from consistent results in two independent YOD1 KO clones showing reduced NF-κB signaling upon YOD1 reconstitution (Figure 5E, 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: TRAF6 knock-down severely impairs IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Whereas knock-down of TRAF6 or p62 severely impaired IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation as evident by EMSA, depletion of YOD1 enhanced NF-κB activation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: p62 knock-down severely impairs IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Whereas knock-down of TRAF6 or p62 severely impaired IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation as evident by EMSA, depletion of YOD1 enhanced NF-κB activation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA in p62 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: YOD1 depletion enhances IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Whereas knock-down of TRAF6 or p62 severely impaired IL-1β triggered NF-κB activation as evident by EMSA, depletion of YOD1 enhanced NF-κB activation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA in YOD1 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 is decreased by TRAF6 knock-down in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Congruently, induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 was decreased by TRAF6 or p62 knock-down and increased by YOD1 knock-down (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 is decreased by p62 knock-down in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Congruently, induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 was decreased by TRAF6 or p62 knock-down and increased by YOD1 knock-down (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in p62 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 is increased by YOD1 knock-down in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Congruently, induction of NF-κB target genes NFKBIA/IκBα and TNFAIP3/A20 was decreased by TRAF6 or p62 knock-down and increased by YOD1 knock-down (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by qRT-PCR in YOD1 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: TRAF6 knock-down prevents IκBα degradation upon IL-1β stimulation in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Downregulation of TRAF6 or p62 prevented IκBα degradation and YOD1 depletion enhanced IκBα removal upon IL-1β stimulation, demonstrating that all proteins affect NF-κB signaling (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: p62 knock-down prevents IκBα degradation upon IL-1β stimulation in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Downregulation of TRAF6 or p62 prevented IκBα degradation and YOD1 depletion enhanced IκBα removal upon IL-1β stimulation, demonstrating that all proteins affect NF-κB signaling (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in p62 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: YOD1 depletion enhances IκBα removal upon IL-1β stimulation in HeLa cells.
claims.source: Downregulation of TRAF6 or p62 prevented IκBα degradation and YOD1 depletion enhanced IκBα removal upon IL-1β stimulation, demonstrating that all proteins affect NF-κB signaling (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot in YOD1 knock-down HeLa cells shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: YOD1 controls IKK activation as YOD1 reduction coincides with increased IKK T-loop phosphorylation after IL-1β treatment.
claims.source: Since TRAF6 acts upstream of IKK on the route to NF-κB, we verified that YOD1 also controls IKK activation by showing that YOD1 reduction coincides with increased IKK T-loop phosphorylation after IL-1β treatment (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis of IKK phosphorylation in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: YOD1 knock-down does not affect the activation of the MAPKs JNK, p38 and ERK upon IL-1β stimulation.
claims.source: Of note, while IKK/NF-κB activation was significantly enhanced in the absence of YOD1, we found no effect of YOD1 knock-down on the activation of the MAPKs JNK, p38 and ERK (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by Western blot analysis of MAPK phosphorylation in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: TRAF6 is involved in NF-κB activation in response to IL-1R stimulation but dispensable for TNFR triggered NF-κB activation.
claims.source: TRAF6 is involved in NF-κB activation in response to IL-1R stimulation, but dispensable for TNFR triggered NF-κB activation (Lomaga et al., 1999; Cao et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature (Lomaga et al., 1999; Cao et al., 1996).

claims.claim: YOD1 depletion leads to strongly augmented NF-κB signaling and activation after IL-1R engagement but not after TNFα stimulation.
claims.source: While both stimuli induced NF-κB activation as evident by IκBα degradation and NF-κB DNA binding, YOD1 depletion led to strongly augmented NF-κB signaling and activation after IL-1R engagement, while TNFα-induced NF-κB signaling was unaffected by altered YOD1 amounts.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA and Western blot comparing IL-1β and TNFα stimulation in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: TNFα-induced NF-κB signaling is unaffected by altered YOD1 amounts.
claims.source: While both stimuli induced NF-κB activation as evident by IκBα degradation and NF-κB DNA binding, YOD1 depletion led to strongly augmented NF-κB signaling and activation after IL-1R engagement, while TNFα-induced NF-κB signaling was unaffected by altered YOD1 amounts.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by EMSA and Western blot comparing IL-1β and TNFα stimulation in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: YOD1 expression does not interfere with TRAF6 poly-ubiquitination under denaturing conditions.
claims.source: Under denaturing conditions (1% SDS) and after MYC-IP, TRAF6 ubiquitination is readily detectable and YOD1 expression did not interfere with TRAF6 poly-ubiquitination, which is in line with its previously reported inability to cleave K63-linked ubiquitin chains (Mevissen et al., 2013) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 7A and supported by citation to previous literature (Mevissen et al., 2013).

claims.claim: YOD1 is unable to cleave K63-linked ubiquitin chains.
claims.source: Under denaturing conditions (1% SDS) and after MYC-IP, TRAF6 ubiquitination is readily detectable and YOD1 expression did not interfere with TRAF6 poly-ubiquitination, which is in line with its previously reported inability to cleave K63-linked ubiquitin chains (Mevissen et al., 2013) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Mevissen et al., 2013) and confirmed by in vitro cleavage assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Binding of p62 enhances TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination.
claims.source: Binding of p62 has been shown to enhance TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination (Wooten et al., 2005) and as expected, TRAF6 ubiquitination was strongly increased in the presence of p62 (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Wooten et al., 2005) and demonstrated by ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Co-expression of YOD1 abrogates the enhancement of TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by p62.
claims.source: Noticeably, co-expression of YOD1 abrogated this enhancement.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S impairs the boost of TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by p62, though not as severely as YOD1 WT.
claims.source: Also, catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S impaired the boost of TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by p62, even though the inhibition was not quite as severe as with YOD1 WT.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay shown in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: Recombinant YOD1 does not cleave TRAF6 ubiquitin chains in vitro.
claims.source: In contrast, neither recombinant YOD1 (K11, K27, K29 and K33 selectivity) nor Cezanne (K11 selectivity) were cleaving TRAF6 ubiquitin chains.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro DUB cleavage assay shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: p62-induced attachment of K63-linked ubiquitin chains to TRAF6 is counterbalanced by YOD1 primarily by a non-catalytic mechanism.
claims.source: Therefore, the data show that p62-induced attachment of K63-linked ubiquitin chains to TRAF6 is counterbalanced by YOD1 primarily by a non-catalytic mechanism that involves competition with p62 for TRAF6 association (compare Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing YOD1 does not cleave K63 chains but competes with p62 for TRAF6 binding (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3E, 3F).

claims.claim: TRAF6 ubiquitination upon IL-1β treatment is diminished upon re-expression of YOD1 in YOD1 KO cells.
claims.source: TRAF6 was ubiquitinated upon IL-1β treatment in mock transduced YOD1 KO HeLa cell clones, but TRAF6 ubiquitination was diminished upon re-expression of YOD1 (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in reconstituted YOD1 KO cells shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: IL-1-induced TRAF6 ubiquitination correlates with decreased binding of YOD1 to TRAF6 after IL-1 stimulation.
claims.source: In fact, IL-1-induced TRAF6 ubiquitination correlates with a decreased binding of YOD1 to TRAF6 after IL-1 stimulation (see Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and we asked, whether reduced binding is also visible at the level of endogenous proteins in HeLa cells and primary HUVEC cells (Figure 7C and D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing time-dependent decrease in YOD1/TRAF6 interaction (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, Figure 7C, 7D).

claims.claim: YOD1 co-precipitates with TRAF6 in unstimulated HeLa cells and the interaction is lost within the first 15–20 min of IL-1β stimulation.
claims.source: As noted earlier, YOD1 was co-precipitating with TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and the interaction was lost within the first 15–20 min of IL-1β stimulation, revealing that TRAF6 is released from YOD1.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation time course in HeLa cells shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: YOD1 co-precipitates with TRAF6 in unstimulated HUVEC and the interaction is lost within the first 15–20 min of IL-1β stimulation.
claims.source: As noted earlier, YOD1 was co-precipitating with TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and the interaction was lost within the first 15–20 min of IL-1β stimulation, revealing that TRAF6 is released from YOD1.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation time course in HUVEC shown in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: p62 depletion completely abolishes stimulus-dependent TRAF6 ubiquitination.
claims.source: Whereas p62 depletion completely abolished stimulus-dependent TRAF6 ubiquitination, down-regulation of YOD1 had an opposite effect, leading to increased ubiquitination after IL-1β treatment.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in p62 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: Down-regulation of YOD1 leads to increased TRAF6 ubiquitination after IL-1β treatment.
claims.source: Whereas p62 depletion completely abolished stimulus-dependent TRAF6 ubiquitination, down-regulation of YOD1 had an opposite effect, leading to increased ubiquitination after IL-1β treatment.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7E.

claims.claim: TRAF6 is primarily modified with K63-linked ubiquitin chains upon IL-1β stimulation.
claims.source: However, none of the other DUBs including YOD1 was able to remove TRAF6 ubiquitin chains, strongly suggesting that TRAF6 is primarily modified with K63-linked ubiquitin chains and that YOD1 is counteracting TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by a non-catalytic mechanism.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro DUB cleavage assay showing K63-specific DUBs cleave TRAF6 ubiquitin chains (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: YOD1 is counteracting TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by a non-catalytic mechanism.
claims.source: However, none of the other DUBs including YOD1 was able to remove TRAF6 ubiquitin chains, strongly suggesting that TRAF6 is primarily modified with K63-linked ubiquitin chains and that YOD1 is counteracting TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination by a non-catalytic mechanism.
claims.evidence: Inferred from inability of YOD1 to cleave TRAF6 ubiquitin chains (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) combined with its ability to prevent p62-enhanced ubiquitination (Figure 7A).

claims.claim: Ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment requires p62.
claims.source: Ubiquitination of the IKK regulatory subunit NEMO is an important step in stimulus-dependent IKK activation and it was shown that NEMO ubiquitination induced by TRAF6 expression or IL-1β stimulation requires p62 (Zotti et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Zotti et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment is abolished in TRAF6 knock-down HeLa cells.
claims.source: Also in HeLa cells ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment was abolished in TRAF6 or p62 knock-down cells and YOD1 depletion had the opposite effect by enhancing stimulus-dependent NEMO ubiquitination (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in TRAF6 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: Ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment is abolished in p62 knock-down HeLa cells.
claims.source: Also in HeLa cells ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment was abolished in TRAF6 or p62 knock-down cells and YOD1 depletion had the opposite effect by enhancing stimulus-dependent NEMO ubiquitination (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in p62 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: YOD1 depletion enhances stimulus-dependent NEMO ubiquitination after IL-1β treatment.
claims.source: Also in HeLa cells ubiquitination of NEMO after IL-1β treatment was abolished in TRAF6 or p62 knock-down cells and YOD1 depletion had the opposite effect by enhancing stimulus-dependent NEMO ubiquitination (Figure 7F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by ubiquitination assay in YOD1 knock-down cells shown in Figure 7F.

claims.claim: YOD1 counteracts IL-1 signaling to NF-κB by functioning as a negative regulator of TRAF6/p62-mediated ubiquitination events.
claims.source: Thus, YOD1 counteracts IL-1 signaling to NF-κB by functioning as a negative regulator of TRAF6/p62-mediated ubiquitination events.
claims.evidence: Inferred from data showing YOD1 prevents p62-enhanced TRAF6 ubiquitination and NEMO ubiquitination (Figure 7A, 7E, 7F).

claims.claim: YOD1 is an OTU domain DUB that can hydrolyze K11, K27, K29 and K33 ubiquitin linkages.
claims.source: YOD1 is an OTU domain DUB that can hydrolyze K11, K27, K29 and K33 ubiquitin linkages (Mevissen et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Mevissen et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Structure-function analyses show a high preference of the YOD1 OTU for K11- and K33-linked ubiquitin.
claims.source: Structure-function analyses showed a high preference of the YOD1 OTU for K11- and K33-linked ubiquitin (Flierman et al., 2016) and as expected, we do not detect cleavage of K63-linked ubiquitin chains generated by TRAF6.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature (Flierman et al., 2016) and confirmed by in vitro cleavage assay (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).

claims.claim: CYLD is acting on TRAF6/p62 complexes but is not preventing the formation of TRAF6/p62 aggregates.
claims.source: As we described here for YOD1, CYLD is acting on TRAF6/p62 complexes, but - in contrast to YOD1 - CYLD is not preventing the formation of TRAF6/p62 aggregates, but is recruited to TRAF6 by p62 (Jin et al., 2008; Wooten et al., 2008).

results.result: YOD1 is a novel direct interactor of TRAF6 that binds specifically to the C-terminal MATH domain through its N-terminal UBX domain, independent of the typical TRAF6 interaction motif (TIM). This interaction is selective for TRAF6 over TRAF2 and occurs in multiple cell types including HEK293, HeLa, U2OS, and primary HUVEC cells.
results.evaluation: The result is well-supported by multiple complementary experimental approaches including yeast two-hybrid assays (C33, C34), in vitro pull-down experiments with recombinant proteins (C42, C43), co-immunoprecipitation in cells with deletion constructs (C48, C49, C50), and endogenous protein interactions across multiple cell types (C55-C58). The specificity for TRAF6 over TRAF2 (C53, C54) and independence from p97 (C60) are also demonstrated. The mapping of interaction domains is consistent across different experimental systems.

results.result: YOD1 competes with p62 for binding to the C-terminal MATH domain of TRAF6 and prevents TRAF6 recruitment to p62 sequestosomes through a non-catalytic mechanism. YOD1, p62, and TRAF6 do not form a trimeric complex.
results.evaluation: The competitive binding is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation showing YOD1 inhibits p62/TRAF6 association while p62 does not affect YOD1/TRAF6 binding (C74, C75). Both proteins bind the same MATH domain (C73). Critically, catalytically inactive YOD1 C160S shows similar effects (C76, C79), establishing the non-catalytic mechanism. Microscopy data showing spatial exclusion of p62 from YOD1/TRAF6 aggregates (C78, C80) supports the competitive model and absence of a trimeric complex (C81).

results.result: YOD1 associates with TRAF6 in unstimulated cells but dissociates within 15-20 minutes of IL-1β stimulation, correlating with increased TRAF6 ubiquitination.
results.evaluation: The stimulus-dependent dissociation is demonstrated by time-course co-immunoprecipitation experiments in both reconstituted YOD1 KO cells (C94, C95) and endogenous proteins in HeLa cells and HUVEC (C123, C124). The correlation with TRAF6 ubiquitination (C122) provides mechanistic insight. The consistent timing across different cell types strengthens the finding.

results.result: YOD1 negatively regulates IL-1β-induced NF-κB signaling independent of its catalytic activity. YOD1 overexpression decreases NF-κB target gene expression and NF-κB activation, while YOD1 depletion or knockout enhances these responses.
results.evaluation: The negative regulatory role is supported by bidirectional experiments: overexpression of both YOD1 WT and catalytically inactive C160S reduces NF-κB target gene expression (C83, C84, C85), while knock-down enhances it (C86, C9). The independence from catalytic activity (C85) is critical and well-demonstrated. Reconstitution experiments in two independent YOD1 KO clones (C96-C99) provide strong genetic evidence. The consistency across multiple experimental systems (overexpression, knock-down, knockout/reconstitution) and readouts (target genes, DNA binding, IκBα degradation) is compelling.

results.result: YOD1 counteracts IL-1β-triggered NF-κB signaling at the level of IKK activation and upstream of IκBα degradation. TRAF6 and p62 are required for IL-1β signaling, while YOD1 depletion enhances it.
results.evaluation: The epistatic relationships are clearly demonstrated: TRAF6 and p62 knock-down severely impair IL-1β signaling (C88, C100, C101, C106, C107), while YOD1 depletion enhances it (C89, C90, C102, C108). The effect on IKK phosphorylation (C109) places YOD1 upstream of IKK activation. The consistency across multiple cell types (iBMDM and HeLa) and multiple readouts (NF-κB DNA binding, target gene expression, IκBα degradation, IKK phosphorylation) strongly supports the model.

results.result: YOD1 specifically regulates IL-1β-induced NF-κB signaling but does not affect TNFα-induced NF-κB signaling or IL-1β-induced MAPK activation, indicating pathway specificity.
results.evaluation: The pathway specificity is demonstrated by direct comparison: YOD1 depletion enhances IL-1β but not TNFα-induced NF-κB signaling (C112, C113), and does not affect MAPK activation (C110, C145). The lack of effect on JNK is consistent with p62's known lack of involvement in JNK activation by TRAF6 (C146, C147). This specificity supports the model that YOD1 selectively acts on p62/TRAF6 complexes.

results.result: YOD1 counteracts TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination and substrate ubiquitination primarily through a non-catalytic mechanism. YOD1 does not cleave K63-linked ubiquitin chains on TRAF6, but prevents p62-enhanced TRAF6 ubiquitination by competing for TRAF6 binding.
results.evaluation: The non-catalytic mechanism is strongly supported by multiple lines of evidence: YOD1 does not cleave K63-linked ubiquitin chains in vitro (C115, C119), YOD1 expression does not reduce existing TRAF6 ubiquitination under denaturing conditions (C114), but YOD1 prevents p62-enhanced ubiquitination (C117) with catalytically inactive C160S showing similar effects (C118). The demonstration that TRAF6 is primarily K63-ubiquitinated (C127) and that YOD1 depletion increases while p62 depletion decreases TRAF6 ubiquitination (C125, C126) supports the competitive model. The reconstitution experiments (C121) provide additional genetic evidence.

results.result: YOD1 negatively regulates NEMO ubiquitination in response to IL-1β stimulation. NEMO ubiquitination requires both TRAF6 and p62, and is enhanced by YOD1 depletion.
results.evaluation: The regulation of NEMO ubiquitination is demonstrated by knock-down experiments showing that TRAF6 and p62 are required (C130, C131) while YOD1 depletion enhances it (C132). This extends the regulatory role of YOD1 beyond TRAF6 auto-ubiquitination to substrate ubiquitination, consistent with the overall model (C133). The data are clear and consistent.

results.result: YOD1 and TRAF6 co-localize to cytosolic speckles upon co-expression in cells, forming larger clusters. This interaction does not require YOD1 catalytic activity.
results.evaluation: The co-localization is demonstrated by confocal microscopy showing overlapping fluorescence signals (C64), enrichment of each protein in the other's spots (C66), and quantitative image analysis (C65). The independence from catalytic activity is shown by similar co-localization with YOD1 C160S (C67). The data provide visual confirmation of the biochemical interaction and support the functional model.

results.result: TRAF6 is recruited to p62 sequestosomes, but YOD1 does not co-localize with p62 aggregates. When all three proteins are co-expressed, YOD1 and TRAF6 co-localize while p62 is largely excluded from YOD1/TRAF6 aggregates.
results.evaluation: The spatial relationships are clearly demonstrated by microscopy: TRAF6 co-localizes with p62 (C69), YOD1 does not co-localize with p62 (C70), and in triple transfections, p62 is excluded from YOD1/TRAF6 clusters (C78). Quantitative image analysis confirms stronger TRAF6 enrichment in YOD1 versus p62 spots (C80). The effect is independent of YOD1 catalytic activity (C79). These data provide strong visual support for the competitive binding model.

results.result: Two independent YOD1 knockout HeLa cell clones were generated by CRISPR/Cas9 and reconstituted with YOD1. Reconstitution restores YOD1/TRAF6 interaction and reduces NF-κB signaling and target gene expression.
results.evaluation: The generation of two independent KO clones (C93) with consistent phenotypes upon reconstitution (C99) provides strong genetic evidence for YOD1's role. The restoration of TRAF6 binding (C94) and reduction in NF-κB signaling (C96, C97, C98) upon reconstitution demonstrates specificity. The use of two independent clones controls for clonal variation and off-target effects.

results.result: YOD1 does not act as a negative regulator of CD40 or RANK signaling in 293 or PC3 cells, and may even promote NF-κB activation in these contexts. The role of p62 in these pathways is cell-type and context-dependent.
results.evaluation: The pathway-specific effects are clearly demonstrated: YOD1 knock-down impairs rather than enhances CD40 and RANK signaling (C150, C151), and p62 knock-down has no significant effect in these cells (C152). The context-dependence is supported by citations to previous literature showing variable p62 effects (C153, C154). This result establishes important boundaries for YOD1's regulatory role and suggests additional complexity in TRAF6 regulation.

results.result: YOD1 acts at an earlier phase of IL-1 signaling compared to the negative regulators CYLD and A20. YOD1 binds TRAF6 in unstimulated cells and is released upon stimulation, while CYLD is recruited by p62 to active TRAF6 and A20 binds only after prolonged stimulation.
results.evaluation: The temporal model is supported by the timing of YOD1/TRAF6 interaction (binding in unstimulated cells, release upon stimulation) (C141) and enhanced early NF-κB signaling upon YOD1 depletion (C142). The comparison to CYLD and A20 is based on well-established literature (C136, C137, C139, C140). The model of sequential negative regulation is logical and consistent with the data, though the speculative component about CYLD compensating for YOD1 loss (C143, C144) is appropriately cautious.

results.result: Background on TRAF6, p62, and YOD1: TRAF6 is an essential E3 ligase in IL-1 signaling that catalyzes K63-linked ubiquitination. p62 enhances TRAF6 activity and recruits CYLD. YOD1 is a DUB that acts as a cofactor for p97 in ERAD.
results.evaluation: These claims establish the relevant background and are supported by appropriate citations to previous literature. They provide necessary context for understanding the novel findings about YOD1's role in TRAF6 regulation.

results.result: Validation of yeast two-hybrid interactions: YOD1 and p97 interaction is confirmed, TRAF6 self-associates and binds UBC13 and A20 but not p97, and YOD1 shows selective binding to TRAF6 and p97 within a panel of E3 ligases. TRAF6 and p97 can bind YOD1 independently.
results.evaluation: These validation experiments confirm known interactions (YOD1/p97) and establish the specificity of YOD1 binding within a panel of ubiquitin system proteins (C40, C41). The demonstration that TRAF6 and p97 bind YOD1 independently (C45, C46, C47) is important for understanding YOD1's multiple functions. The data are clear and well-controlled.

results.result: Discussion of YOD1's mechanism and relationship to other TRAF6 regulators: YOD1/TRAF6 binding is independent of p97, occurs in unstimulated cells without requiring TRAF6 oligomerization, and YOD1 raises the threshold for TRAF6/p62 signaling. YOD1 can counteract TRAF6 recruitment to sequestosomes.
results.evaluation: These interpretive claims synthesize the experimental findings into a coherent model. The independence from p97 (C157) is experimentally demonstrated. The binding in unstimulated cells (C166) and ability to prevent sequestosome recruitment (C174) are well-supported by data. The interpretation that YOD1 raises the signaling threshold (C168) is a reasonable inference from the competitive binding and functional data. The discussion appropriately integrates the findings with established knowledge about sequestosomes (C170-C173).
